gloss_terse: pierce, bore through (especially the ear in a ceremony of perpetual servitude)
gloss_readable: This verb appears in the ceremonial context of Exodus 21:6, where a servant who voluntarily chooses to remain with his master has his ear pierced as a permanent mark of service. The act combines physical action with deep symbolic significance—the pierced ear signifies willing, lifelong commitment. The multilingual evidence (Spanish 'horadará,' English 'pierce') consistently captures the physical penetration, though the profound relational dimension requires the full context to appreciate.

senses.1: The single occurrence in Exodus 21:6 describes the ceremonial piercing of a servant's ear with an awl, marking his choice to remain with his master permanently. This is not casual injury but ritualized commitment—the physical mark embodying the servant's declaration 'I love my master.' Cross-linguistic glosses uniformly emphasize the penetrating action, pointing to the concrete, irreversible nature of this covenant sign.

gloss_terse: fitted out, inlaid, arranged (of interior decoration or paving)
gloss_readable: This rare verb appears only in Song of Songs 3:10, describing Solomon's palanquin whose interior is 'fitted out with love.' The Hebrew root suggests careful arrangement or fitting together of materials, perhaps inlaid work or paving. The textual uncertainty reflects ancient translators' struggles with this technical term. The romantic context transforms architectural language into metaphor—the physical craftsmanship becomes an image of devotion.

senses.1: In Song 3:10, this passive participle describes the interior of Solomon's ornate carriage. The glosses range from 'inlaid' (English) to 'paved' (French) to 'upholstered' (Spanish 'tapizado'), all suggesting decorative finish work. The phrase 'fitted out with love' (rather than precious materials) creates beautiful ambiguity—is love the craftsman or the material? The cognate languages point to joining or arranging elements in sequence.

gloss_terse: hot stones, heated rocks (used for baking)
gloss_readable: These are glowing or heated stones, appearing in 1 Kings 19:6 where the exhausted Elijah finds bread baked on hot stones prepared by an angel. The term emphasizes the stones' heat, not merely their substance. This detail enriches the narrative—not just bread but freshly baked bread, still warm from the coals. The divine provision includes culinary care. Multilingual glosses uniformly capture the 'hot' quality, distinguishing these from ordinary stones.

senses.1: The plural 'hot stones' in 1 Kings 19:6 refers to the traditional baking method where bread dough is placed on heated stones. The angel's provision for Elijah includes this warm, fresh-baked bread ('cake of hot stones'). Every major translation preserves the thermal element: Spanish 'carbones' (coals), English 'hot stones,' emphasizing that these aren't cold rocks but heat-retaining cooking surfaces. Related to the glowing stones in Isaiah 6:6, though lexically distinct.

gloss_terse: burning coal, live coal (from the altar)
gloss_readable: This singular form designates a live coal, appearing in Isaiah's throne vision (6:6) where a seraph uses tongs to take a burning coal from the altar and touch the prophet's lips for purification. The coal's heat matters—it's not ash but active fire, potent enough to cauterize sin. The image combines danger and cleansing: what could destroy instead sanctifies. Though lexically related to H7529, this refers to glowing coals rather than heated baking stones.

senses.1: In Isaiah 6:6, the seraph takes this burning coal from the altar with tongs—too hot for direct handling. The coal's heat effects purification of Isaiah's unclean lips. Spanish 'brasa' (ember) and English 'burning coal' both emphasize the live, glowing state. This is sacramental fire, transforming guilt into readiness for prophetic service. The vision pairs physical impossibility (touching live coals) with spiritual necessity (cleansing from sin).

gloss_readable: This noun denotes rottenness or decay, appearing in Job 41:27 (English 41:19) where Leviathan regards iron as 'rotten wood'—utterly contemptible and ineffective. The term emphasizes advanced decomposition, wood so decayed it has lost all structural integrity. In this context, rottenness becomes a metaphor for worthlessness: even strong iron is, to Leviathan, as useless as punk wood. The multilingual evidence (Spanish 'podrida') consistently captures the decay aspect.

senses.1: Job 41:27 uses this vivid image in God's speech about Leviathan's invulnerability: to this creature, iron weapons are no more threatening than 'wood of rottenness.' The phrase evokes completely degraded timber—spongy, crumbling, powerless. Spanish 'podrida' (rotten) precisely captures the state. The rhetorical force lies in the reversal: iron, symbol of strength, is dismissed as thoroughly as decomposed wood. Leviathan's superiority makes the strong seem pathetically weak.

gloss_terse: Rakkon (place name: town in Dan's territory)
gloss_readable: This is a place name appearing in Joshua's boundary descriptions for the tribe of Dan (19:46). The site is likely identical with the nearby Yarkon, as suggested by the similar consonants and the fact that the Septuagint omits it (possibly viewing it as a textual variant). The exact location remains uncertain, though Jewish tradition later connected it with the region near Tiberias. The conjunction 'and' before the name integrates it into the boundary list.

senses.1: In Joshua 19:46, 'ha-Rakkon' appears in the territorial allotment for Dan, listed among cities and geographical features. Modern scholars see this as probably a doublet of 'the Yarkon' (the river that flows through modern Tel Aviv). The multilingual glosses preserve the Hebrew article 'ha-' and the name 'Rakkon,' treating it as a geographical designation rather than translating it. The uncertainty in ancient versions reflects early scribal puzzlement over this reference.

gloss_readable: This term refers to spiced or aromatic wine, appearing in Song of Songs 8:2 where the beloved speaks of giving her lover 'wine of spice'—wine infused with aromatic ingredients. Ancient spiced wines were prestigious luxury items, enhanced with various aromatics for flavor and fragrance. The definite article suggests a specific type: 'the spiced (wine).' This detail enriches the love poetry with sensory abundance: not plain wine but perfumed, carefully prepared wine, expressing lavish affection.

senses.1: In Song 8:2, 'the spiced' (with 'wine' implied or explicit) describes aromatic wine the bride would give her beloved. Spanish 'especiado' (spiced), French 'aromatisé' (aromatized), all capture the enhancement through aromatic additives. This was ancient viticulture's luxury product—wine improved with spices, creating complex flavors and fragrances. The context of extravagant love-language makes this detail fitting: the best, most carefully crafted refreshment for the beloved.

gloss_terse: perfumers, makers of ointments and fragrances (professional guild)
gloss_readable: This plural noun designates professional perfumers or ointment-makers, appearing in Nehemiah 3:8 where Hananiah 'son of the perfumers' (i.e., member of the perfumers' guild) helps rebuild Jerusalem's wall. The phrase 'son of the perfumers' indicates guild membership, a common way to denote professional association in ancient contexts. These artisans specialized in creating the precious oils, incenses, and perfumes essential for temple worship, royal courts, and daily life in the ancient Near East.

senses.1: Nehemiah 3:8 mentions 'one of the perfumers' (literally 'son of the perfumers'), identifying Hananiah by his professional guild. The multilingual glosses uniformly preserve the occupational designation: Spanish 'perfumeros,' English 'perfumers.' These specialists compounded the complex recipes for sacred anointing oil, incense, and cosmetic preparations. The detail that even perfumers joined the wall-building effort shows the comprehensive mobilization of Jerusalem's population for Nehemiah's restoration project.

gloss_readable: This plural noun refers to perfumes or fragrant ointments, appearing only in Isaiah 57:9 in a scathing denunciation of idolatry. The passage describes bringing perfumes (along with oil) to a pagan deity. The use of precious cosmetics in illicit worship heightens the prophetic critique—Israel lavishes on false gods the fragrances that should honor Yahweh alone. The second-person suffix ('your perfumes') personalizes the indictment, making the idolatry intimate and deliberate.

senses.1: Isaiah 57:9 condemns those who bring 'your perfumes' to idols, wasting precious aromatic preparations on false worship. Spanish 'tus perfumes' (your perfumes) preserves both the possessive and the plural. These would be expensive fragrant oils or ointments, valuable trade goods. The prophet's point cuts deep: Israel takes what should express devotion to God and instead offers it to worthless idols. The costly perfumes underscore the tragic misdirection of worship.

gloss_terse: perfumers (female), women who make fragrances and ointments
gloss_readable: This feminine plural noun designates female perfumers or ointment-makers, appearing in 1 Samuel 8:13 where Samuel warns that a future king will conscript Israelite daughters as perfumers, cooks, and bakers for the royal court. The grouping with other culinary and aromatic specialists suggests these women would produce the luxury goods required by monarchy—fragrant oils, cosmetics, and incense. The warning presents royal service as burdensome appropriation of family members.

senses.1: In 1 Samuel 8:13, Samuel's dire preview of kingship includes the seizure of daughters 'for perfumers, for cooks, and for bakers.' The Spanish 'para perfumeras' (for perfumers-feminine) preserves the gender specificity. These women would staff the royal production of fragrances and ointments, work that in household contexts women often managed. The threefold list (perfumers, cooks, bakers) evokes the extensive domestic infrastructure monarchy would require, transforming free daughters into royal servants.

gloss_readable: This plural construct noun refers to hammered or beaten-out metal plates, appearing in Numbers 16:38 (English 17:3) where the censers of Korah's rebels are to be hammered into sheets for plating the altar. The term emphasizes the process: metal beaten thin and wide, transformed from vessels into covering plates. This becomes a perpetual memorial—rebellion's instruments converted into sanctuary furnishings, warning against future presumption. The hammering itself is sacramental: judgment transformed into instruction.

senses.1: Numbers 16:38 commands that the bronze censers be made into 'hammered plates' (literally 'expansions of plates') to overlay the altar. The glosses emphasize the hammering process: Spanish 'láminas' (sheets/plates), English 'hammered.' The rebels' censers, used in unauthorized worship that brought death, become permanent altar covering—visible reminder that holiness cannot be presumed upon. The metal's transformation from censers to plates mirrors the narrative's transformation from rebellion to warning.

gloss_readable: This verb means to spit, appearing in Leviticus 15:8 in purity regulations: if a man with a discharge spits on someone clean, that person becomes unclean. Spitting here is not hostile but physiological—yet it transmits impurity. The law's precision about even saliva shows how comprehensively discharge-related uncleanness could spread. The regulation protects community health while maintaining ritual boundaries, treating spittle as a vector for contagion.

senses.1: Leviticus 15:8 addresses the scenario where 'the one with the discharge spits on the clean person'—direct transmission of impurity through saliva. The verb appears with the preposition 'upon,' indicating the target. Spanish 'escupiere' (should spit), English 'spits' capture the physiological act. This isn't contemptuous spitting (as in some other biblical contexts) but the ordinary expectoration that becomes significant because it carries ritual impurity from the diseased person to the clean.

gloss_terse: Rakkath (place name: fortified city in Naphtali's territory)
gloss_readable: This is a place name, one of the fortified cities in Naphtali's allotment (Joshua 19:35). Jewish tradition later identified it with Tiberias on the Sea of Galilee's western shore, though this identification remains uncertain. The Septuagint's variant spellings reflect ancient uncertainty about the exact location. As a fortified city, Rakkath would have been strategically important in Naphtali's northern territory, helping secure the tribe's holdings.

senses.1: Joshua 19:35 lists Rakkath among Naphtali's fortified cities, situated in the northern tribal territory. The multilingual glosses simply transliterate: Spanish 'Racat,' English 'Rakkath.' Later Jewish tradition connected this site with Tiberias, the important Galilean city that became a center of rabbinic learning. The Septuagint's various renderings suggest the translators struggled with this proper name. The designation 'fortified city' indicates Rakkath's strategic and defensive significance in Naphtali's territorial network.

gloss_readable: This noun means permission or authorization, appearing only in Ezra 3:7 where the returned exiles give money and provisions to workers 'according to the permission of Cyrus.' The term denotes official royal authorization—not mere tolerance but explicit grant. This legal precision matters in Ezra's narrative: the restoration happens not as rebellion but as imperially sanctioned project. The Persian king's written permission validates the temple rebuilding, protecting it from local opposition.

senses.1: Ezra 3:7 describes provision of supplies 'according to the grant of Cyrus king of Persia'—the royal authorization that legitimizes the entire restoration enterprise. Spanish 'según autorización' (according to authorization) captures the formal, legal character. This isn't informal approval but documented permission, likely referring to Cyrus's famous decree allowing the Jews to return and rebuild. The phrase grounds the restoration in official sanction, making opposition to it resistance to imperial policy.

gloss_readable: This passive participle means 'inscribed' or 'written down,' appearing in Daniel 10:21 where the angelic messenger tells Daniel he will declare 'what is inscribed in the writing of truth.' The term emphasizes permanent recording—not oral tradition but fixed text. The 'writing of truth' suggests an authoritative divine document, a heavenly archive where future events are already recorded. This apocalyptic image presents history as foreordained and documented, revelation as disclosure of what's already written.

senses.1: Daniel 10:21 speaks of 'that which is inscribed in the writing of truth'—the definite article marking this as a specific, authoritative text. Spanish 'lo escrito' (that which is written), French 'écrire' (to write), all emphasize the written, recorded nature. The passive participle suggests something already permanently documented. In apocalyptic literature, this imagery of heavenly books recording future events portrays divine sovereignty: history unfolds according to what's already inscribed in God's archive.

gloss_readable: This is a personal name appearing in 1 Chronicles 7:25, part of the genealogy of Ephraim. The name Resheph is identical to a common noun meaning 'flame' or 'burning,' and also to a West Semitic deity associated with plague and the underworld. Whether the personal name carries these associations or is simply a theophoric element is uncertain. The genealogical context situates this Resheph within Ephraim's lineage without additional biographical detail.

senses.1: In 1 Chronicles 7:25, Resheph appears as a descendant in Ephraim's genealogy, listed simply by name without further information. The Septuagint transliterates variously, reflecting the challenge of rendering Hebrew names into Greek. The name itself means 'flame' and was also a deity name in Canaanite religion, though in personal names such meanings often become merely conventional. The Chronicles genealogist includes Resheph to establish Ephraimite lineage, particularly leading toward Joshua (the chapter's climactic figure).

gloss_readable: This plural noun with suffix means 'its boilings,' appearing in Ezekiel 24:5 in a prophetic allegory where Jerusalem is depicted as a cooking pot. The command is to 'boil its boilings'—make it boil vigorously. However, BDB notes this is likely a textual corruption for 'its pieces' (the meat inside), which fits better with the cooking metaphor elsewhere in the chapter. The image of intense boiling suits the context of judgment: Jerusalem under siege is like a pot brought to furious, destructive boil.

senses.1: Ezekiel 24:5 uses this phrase in the extended metaphor of Jerusalem as a corroded pot on the fire: 'boil its boilings' or 'make it seethe vigorously.' Spanish 'hervores de ella' (its boilings) preserves the intensified action. Most scholars suspect textual corruption here (reading 'its pieces' instead), but the received text creates vivid image: repeated boiling, fierce heat, destructive intensity—all figuring the siege's relentless pressure. The cooking imagery throughout Ezekiel 24 turns domestic activity into vehicle for judgment oracle.

gloss_terse: harness, bind, attach (animals to a chariot)
gloss_readable: This verb means to harness or attach draft animals to a vehicle, appearing only in Micah 1:13: 'Harness the chariot to the horse.' The command is directed to Lachish in a context of judgment, possibly ironic—prepare to flee, or perhaps prepare for futile military response. The Arabic cognate suggests binding or tying as a reminder, and here the binding is the practical attachment of horse to chariot. The imperative creates urgency: action required in crisis.

senses.1: Micah 1:13 commands the inhabitants of Lachish: 'Harness the chariot to the swift steed.' Spanish 'Unce' (harness/yoke), English 'harness' capture the action of binding animal to vehicle. This could be preparation for flight or battle, though in context it appears futile—Lachish will fall despite chariots. The singular imperative personalizes the address, as if speaking to the city itself. The chariot imagery is bitterly appropriate: Lachish's military strength will not save it from the coming judgment.

gloss_readable: This plural construct noun refers to chains, appearing in Isaiah 40:19 in a description of idol-making: the craftsman overlays the idol with gold 'and chains of silver' (or possibly 'casts silver chains for it'). The context is satirical—the prophet mocks the elaborate process of manufacturing gods. Whether these chains are ornamental decoration or structural fasteners is unclear, but they represent additional costly materials lavished on worthless idols. The silver chains ironically bind not the idol but its deluded worshipers.

senses.1: Isaiah 40:19 describes idol manufacture, mentioning 'chains of silver' as part of the elaborate decoration. Spanish 'y cadenas' (and chains) preserves the connective and plural. The chains likely ornament the idol, adding silver to the gold overlay—expensive materials wasted on handmade deities. The prophet's rhetoric is devastating: such elaborate effort to create a god who can't speak, move, or save. The chains, meant to beautify, become symbols of the craftsmen's bondage to their own handiwork.

gloss_readable: This noun denotes trembling or terror, appearing in Hosea 13:1 in a difficult text: 'When Ephraim spoke, trembling' (or possibly 'spoke with trembling,' or 'spoke, there was trembling'). The verse contrasts Ephraim's former exalted status (when his words commanded fear/respect) with his subsequent guilt through Baal worship. Whether the trembling is Ephraim's own reverent fear or others' fearful response to his authority remains textually ambiguous, but the image evokes a time when Ephraim's leadership carried weight.

senses.1: Hosea 13:1 presents interpretive challenges, but describes a time 'when Ephraim spoke, trembling'—either Ephraim spoke with humble fear, or his speech inspired trembling in others. Spanish 'temblor,' French 'crainte' (fear) both capture the fearful aspect. The verse mourns Ephraim's fall from a state where speaking carried authority/reverence to one of death through idolatry. The trembling represents either proper fear before God (now abandoned) or commanding respect (now lost). Either way, it marks a vanished condition.

gloss_readable: This Hithpael participle means gazing or staring intently, appearing in Genesis 24:21 where Abraham's servant watches Rebekah closely at the well, silently assessing whether the Lord has made his journey successful. The intensive stem suggests sustained, focused attention—not a glance but a gaze. The servant's silence and steady watching create narrative tension: will this be the woman? The multilingual evidence consistently emphasizes the visual focus, the concentrated observation.

senses.1: Genesis 24:21 describes Abraham's servant 'gazing at her' (at Rebekah) after she has offered water to him and his camels—precisely the sign he requested. The Hithpael form intensifies the action: he's staring, watching intently, 'keeping silence to know whether the Lord had made his journey successful.' Spanish 'asombrado' (amazed) adds emotional dimension, though the verb primarily means to gaze steadily. This is the silent, hopeful scrutiny of someone watching for divine confirmation in human actions.

gloss_readable: This noun (Ketiv reading) refers to a devastating storm or ruin, appearing in Proverbs 1:27 where Wisdom warns that calamity will come 'like a storm.' The Qere reading prefers a different vocalization (שׁוֹאָה), but both point to destructive tempest. The image parallels 'whirlwind,' creating vivid picture of sudden, overwhelming disaster. Wisdom's discourse uses storm-language to warn the simple: reject instruction and calamity will strike with meteorological violence and inevitability.

senses.1: Proverbs 1:27 (Ketiv reading) warns that disaster will come upon the foolish 'like a devastating storm,' parallel with 'like a whirlwind.' The multilingual glosses mark this as a textual variant. The imagery is of sudden, irresistible destruction—storm as metaphor for calamity that sweeps away those who ignored Wisdom's call. Whether read as שַׁאֲוָה or שׁוֹאָה (Qere), the term evokes violent weather that obliterates everything in its path, suiting Wisdom's rhetoric of inevitable consequences.

gloss_terse: Shaulite (gentilic: descendants of Shaul, clan in Simeon)
gloss_readable: This is a gentilic adjective (with the definite article) functioning as a collective noun, referring to the Shaulite clan descended from Shaul within the tribe of Simeon. It appears in Numbers 26:13 in the wilderness census, where Israelite families are enumerated. The form follows standard patterns for clan designation, deriving from the ancestor's name with the -ite ending. The article makes it collective: 'the Shaulites' as a group.

senses.1: Numbers 26:13 lists 'the Shaulites' among Simeonite clans in the census. The multilingual glosses transliterate with the appropriate article: Spanish 'los saulitas' (the Shaulites), English 'the Shaulite.' This collective designation identifies all descendants of Shaul son of Simeon as a single clan unit for census and inheritance purposes. The census context makes clan membership crucial—these genealogical distinctions determined land allotment, military organization, and social identity in Israel.

gloss_readable: This noun means ruin or desolation, appearing in Isaiah 24:12, a late oracle depicting universal devastation: 'In the city is left desolation, and the gate is battered into ruin.' The term emphasizes the aftermath—not the destroying but the state of being destroyed. Isaiah 24's apocalyptic vision presents comprehensive collapse, and this word captures the endpoint: emptiness, wreckage, the stillness after catastrophe. The conjunction links this ruin to the broader scene of destruction.

senses.1: Isaiah 24:12 describes the ruined city's condition: 'In the city is left desolation, and the gate is battered into ruin.' Spanish 'y ruina' (and ruin) preserves the conjunction connecting this to the previous devastation. The term denotes the post-destruction state—the silence and emptiness after calamity. In Isaiah 24's cosmic judgment scene, this ruin is not one city's fate but representative of universal collapse. The battered gate particularly symbolizes failed defense, the city's protective boundary now rubble.

gloss_terse: Sheal (personal name: man who married foreign wife)
gloss_readable: This is a personal name appearing in Ezra 10:29, identifying one of the Israelites who had married foreign women during the exile and were required to divorce them in Ezra's reforms. The name itself means 'asking' or 'request.' Beyond this single mention in the list of those with foreign wives, nothing else is known about this individual. The Septuagint renders it variously, reflecting the challenges of transliterating Hebrew names.

senses.1: Ezra 10:29 lists Sheal among those who 'had taken foreign wives'—the controversial marriages Ezra demanded be dissolved to maintain covenant purity. The name appears with the conjunction 'and,' integrating it into the catalog of offenders. German 'und fragte' (and asked) attempts to translate the name's meaning rather than transliterate, showing the semantic root. The list itself is painful: names without stories, men whose personal lives became battleground in the community's struggle to maintain distinct identity after exile.

gloss_readable: This Aramaic noun means request, petition, or affair, appearing in Daniel 4:17 (Aramaic 4:14) in Nebuchadnezzar's dream decree: 'This sentence is by the decree of the watchers, the decision by the word of the holy ones, to the intent that the living may know...' The emphatic form (with Aramaic definite article) marks this as 'the request/matter at hand.' The term has shifted from 'question' to 'affair' or 'matter'—the issue being decided, the case under consideration.

senses.1: Daniel 4:17 (Aramaic section) uses this term for 'the request' or 'the matter' decreed by the heavenly watchers—the sentence upon Nebuchadnezzar. Spanish 'la demanda' (the petition/request), English 'the request' both preserve the definite article. Though the root means 'ask' or 'inquire,' here it's weakened to mean 'affair' or 'matter'—the business at hand. The heavenly council's decree becomes a legal petition presented to the living: this judgment demonstrates that the Most High rules over human kingdoms.

gloss_readable: This personal name means 'I have asked God' or 'God's request,' appearing frequently in post-exilic texts as the father of Zerubbabel, the governor who led the return from Babylon. Ezra 5:2 specifically mentions Shealtiel in connection with the temple rebuilding. The name's theophoric element (containing 'El' = God) reflects piety and dependence. Shealtiel's prominence derives from his son Zerubbabel, the Davidic heir who became focal point for messianic hopes during the restoration.

senses.1: Ezra 5:2 identifies Zerubbabel as 'son of Shealtiel,' the genealogical connection establishing Davidic lineage and legitimacy for leadership. The multilingual glosses transliterate the name: Spanish 'Salatiel,' English 'Shealtiel,' German 'Schealtiel.' Shealtiel appears in both Ezra-Nehemiah and Haggai-Zechariah as Zerubbabel's father, anchoring the governor's authority in Davidic descent. The name itself ('I have asked God') may reflect circumstances of his birth or his parents' piety, a permanent testimony to dependence on divine providence.

gloss_readable: This Qal participle with second feminine suffix means 'those plundering you,' appearing in Jeremiah 30:16 in an oracle of reversal: 'All who devour you shall be devoured, and all your foes shall go into captivity; those who plunder you shall become plunder.' The verb denotes violent seizure and despoiling. The poetic justice is perfect: the plunderers will be plundered. This Ketiv form is marked as Aramaic spelling, showing linguistic influence during the exilic period.

senses.1: Jeremiah 30:16 promises reversal of Israel's suffering: 'those plundering you shall become plunder.' The participle with suffix personalizes the promise—'YOUR plunderers' will face their own despoiling. This is the lex talionis applied to nations: the violence done to Israel will return upon the perpetrators. The Aramaic spelling (Ketiv, versus Hebrew Qere) reflects the linguistic environment of the exile, when Aramaic increasingly influenced Hebrew. The promise offers hope: current plundering is not final; the plunderers face divine judgment.

gloss_terse: flesh, meat; near kin, blood relative
gloss_readable: This noun means flesh, used both literally (as meat or bodily flesh) and figuratively (as blood relation). In Leviticus 18:17 it appears in the prohibition against marrying both a woman and her daughter: 'they are her near relatives'—literally 'her flesh.' The term emphasizes the physical, biological connection—shared blood and kinship. The marriage prohibitions in Leviticus 18 repeatedly invoke this language of 'flesh,' treating sexual relations with close kin as violations of fundamental boundaries.

senses.1: Leviticus 18:17 forbids marrying a woman and her daughter because 'they are her near relatives'—literally 'they are her flesh.' The phrase establishes blood connection as the reason for prohibition: these relationships are too close, the shared kinship creating incestuous overlap. Spanish 'su carne' (her flesh) preserves the literal Hebrew. This usage extends 'flesh' from physical substance to kinship category, treating biological connection as defining relational boundaries. The flesh-language makes abstract kinship viscerally concrete.

gloss_terse: Sheerah (personal name: daughter of Ephraim or his descendant)
gloss_readable: This is a feminine personal name appearing in 1 Chronicles 7:24, identifying a daughter (or female descendant) of Ephraim who built three towns: Lower and Upper Beth-horon and Uzzen-sheerah. She is the only woman in biblical genealogies credited with founding cities, making her remarkable. The name may be related to the word for 'flesh' or 'kinship,' though its precise etymology is uncertain. The Septuagint struggled with this name, rendering it variously.

senses.1: 1 Chronicles 7:24 identifies Sheerah as Ephraim's daughter who 'built Lower and Upper Beth-horon, and Uzzen-sheerah.' The multilingual glosses transliterate: Spanish 'Seera,' English 'Sheerah.' This unique notice makes Sheerah extraordinary in biblical record—a woman credited with founding multiple settlements. Whether biological daughter or more distant descendant is debated, but the text honors her as builder and founder. Uzzen-sheerah ('ear/corner of Sheerah') perpetuates her name geographically, rare recognition for a woman's accomplishment.

gloss_readable: This is the symbolic name of Isaiah's son, appearing in Isaiah 7:3 where God commands the prophet to take this son when confronting King Ahaz. The name means 'a remnant shall return,' embodying Isaiah's theology of judgment and hope—though most will be destroyed, a faithful remnant will survive and return. The child becomes a walking prophecy, his very name proclaiming both threat and promise every time it's spoken. Such naming makes theology incarnate.

senses.1: Isaiah 7:3 introduces 'Shear-jashub your son' whom Isaiah must bring to meet Ahaz during the Syro-Ephraimite crisis. The name means 'a remnant shall return,' a compressed theology: judgment will come but not total annihilation; a purified remnant will survive. The multilingual glosses preserve the Hebrew name untranslated (Spanish 'Shear-Yashub'), recognizing it as proper name with embedded meaning. The son's presence physically embodies the prophetic message: faith or fear? The name confronts Ahaz with both warning and hope.

gloss_readable: This noun's meaning is disputed—possibly devastation or the din/tumult of battle. It appears in Lamentations 3:47, paired with 'ruin' in the poet's lament: 'Terror and the pit have come upon us, devastation and destruction.' The parallelism with 'ruin' suggests catastrophic disaster. Some derive it from roots meaning 'battle-din' or 'uproar,' others from roots meaning 'desolation.' Either sense fits Lamentations' context of Jerusalem's fall. The uncertainty reflects textual difficulty and the word's rarity.

senses.1: Lamentations 3:47 pairs this term with 'ruin' in catalog of disasters: 'fear and the pit, devastation and destruction' (or possibly 'tumult and ruin'). The definite article marks it as specific catastrophe—THE devastation. Whether understanding it as 'battle-din' (the terrible noise of conquest) or 'devastation' (the resulting desolation), the context is Jerusalem's destruction. The poet piles up disaster-terms, and this word—whatever its precise nuance—adds to the overwhelming sense of comprehensive calamity.

gloss_terse: Sabeans (gentilic: people from Sheba, in Arabia)
gloss_readable: This gentilic plural refers to the Sabeans, people from Sheba in southwestern Arabia (modern Yemen), appearing in Joel 3:8 in an oracle of judgment: Israel's oppressors will be sold 'to the Sabeans, to a nation far away.' The Sabeans were known for trade, especially in spices and precious goods. The irony: those who enslaved Israel will themselves be sold to distant traders. The phrase 'far away' emphasizes exile and distance—the oppressors will experience the displacement they inflicted.

senses.1: Joel 3:8 (English 4:8) declares that Judah and Jerusalem will sell their enemies 'to the Sabeans, to a nation far away'—the slave trade reversed. Spanish 'a sabeos' (to Sabeans), French 'Sabéen' preserve the gentilic designation. The Sabeans, from southwestern Arabia, were merchants and traders; being sold to them means entering the international slave trade, experiencing the commodity status Israel suffered. The geographic distance ('far away') compounds the judgment: total removal from homeland, ironic reversal of the scattering inflicted on God's people.

gloss_readable: This plural noun probably means splinters or fragments, appearing in Hosea 8:6 in judgment against the golden calf of Samaria: 'it shall be broken in pieces' (literally 'it shall become splinters'). The image is of complete fragmentation—the idol reduced to shards and fragments, utterly destroyed. The term evokes not just breaking but disintegration into many small pieces. The golden calf, crafted by human hands, will be smashed into splinters, demonstrating its utter powerlessness.

senses.1: Hosea 8:6 pronounces doom on Samaria's calf-idol: 'it shall become splinters'—complete fragmentation. Spanish 'pedazos' (pieces/fragments) captures the multiplication of broken parts. The image reverses creation: what craftsmen assembled will be shattered into countless fragments. The splinters represent both physical destruction and theological point—this 'god' crafted from precious metal has no divine substance, just material that breaks. The calf's fate as splinters mocks the worship that treated metal as deity.

gloss_readable: This is the Aramaic plural construct for 'tribes,' appearing in Ezra 6:17 in the account of the second temple's dedication, where sacrifices are offered 'for all Israel, twelve he-goats, according to the number of the tribes of Israel.' The Aramaic form appears in the Aramaic section of Ezra, though the concept mirrors Hebrew usage. The twelve-tribe structure remains fundamental even after exile, the ritual acknowledging all Israel despite the physical return of only some tribes.

senses.1: Ezra 6:17 describes dedication sacrifices 'according to the number of the tribes of Israel'—twelve he-goats for twelve tribes. The multilingual glosses preserve the construct form: Spanish 'las tribus de' (the tribes of). This is Aramaic equivalent of Hebrew 'tribes,' appearing in Ezra's Aramaic section. The twelve-fold sacrifice honors the ideal of all Israel, even though only Judah, Benjamin, and some Levites returned. The ritual asserts continuity: despite exile and decimation, Israel remains the twelve-tribe people of covenant.

gloss_readable: This is the name of the eleventh month in the post-exilic calendar, corresponding roughly to February-March. It appears in Zechariah 1:7, dating a vision 'on the twenty-fourth day of the eleventh month, which is the month Shebat.' This is a Babylonian loan-word, adopted during the exile to replace earlier Hebrew month names. The etymology possibly relates to Akkadian words for striking or destroying (referring to destructive winter rains), though this remains uncertain.

senses.1: Zechariah 1:7 dates a prophetic vision 'in the month Shebat, which is the eleventh month'—mid-winter in the second year of Darius. The multilingual glosses transliterate: Spanish 'Sebat,' French 'Schebat.' This Babylonian month name replaced earlier Hebrew designations, linguistic evidence of exile's cultural impact. The month falls in winter's heart, when destructive rains dominate Palestine. Zechariah's visions come during this dark, wet season, the timing perhaps reflecting Israel's own dark season of subjugation and partial restoration.

gloss_terse: captive (feminine adjective, describing one in captivity)
gloss_readable: This feminine adjective means 'captive,' appearing in Isaiah 52:2 in an imperative to personified Jerusalem: 'Shake yourself from the dust, arise, O captive Jerusalem!' The feminine form matches 'daughter of Zion,' treating the city as a woman in bondage who must now assert her freedom. The term emphasizes state not just event—not the act of capturing but the condition of being captive. The command to 'arise' and shake off dust calls the captive to agency and restoration.

senses.1: Isaiah 52:2 (based on textual emendation) addresses Jerusalem as 'captive daughter of Zion,' calling her to rise from the dust. The feminine adjective 'captive' matches the feminine personification of the city. Spanish 'cautiva' preserves the gender. The passage demands action from the captive: though enslaved, Jerusalem must now shake off the bonds and dust, asserting freedom in response to God's deliverance. The captive state is real but not final—the call to 'arise' transforms passive victim into active participant in liberation.

gloss_terse: Shobi (personal name: Ammonite who aided David)
gloss_readable: This personal name identifies an Ammonite who brought supplies to David when he fled from Absalom, appearing in 2 Samuel 17:27. Shobi son of Nahash from Rabbah of the Ammonites joined Barzillai and Machir in provisioning David's company during the rebellion. His Ammonite identity is striking—a foreigner showing loyalty when David's own son rebelled. The name may relate to 'captive' or 'captivity,' though its precise meaning is uncertain.

senses.1: 2 Samuel 17:27 lists Shobi among three men who brought essential supplies to David at Mahanaim during Absalom's revolt. The Septuagint renders the name variously, struggling with the Hebrew. What's remarkable is Shobi's Ammonite identity—traditional enemy showing compassion to David in crisis. This foreigner's loyalty contrasts sharply with Israelite Absalom's rebellion. The conjunction 'and Shobi' integrates him into the list of benefactors, honored in Scripture for kindness when David most needed it.

gloss_readline: This noun means flame or blaze, appearing in Job 18:5 in Bildad's description of the wicked person's fate: 'the light of the wicked is put out, and the flame of his fire does not shine.' The parallel structure equates 'light' with 'flame,' both representing the wicked person's life or prosperity. The construct form 'flame of his fire' emphasizes the burning aspect—not just fire but its bright, active flame. The extinction of this flame pictures complete cessation of the wicked person's vitality.

senses.1: Job 18:5 declares that 'the flame of his fire shall not shine,' parallel with 'the light of the wicked goes out.' Spanish 'chispa de' (spark of) varies slightly, but the image is of flame extinguished—the bright, dancing fire reduced to nothing. The construct 'flame of his fire' intensifies the loss: not just fire dimming but its very flame—the most visible, energetic part—disappearing. In wisdom literature, such extinction metaphorically represents death or divine judgment cutting off the wicked person's life and legacy.

gloss_readable: This personal name appears in 1 Chronicles 8:10 in the genealogy of Benjamin, listed among the sons of Shaharaim. The name's spelling varies in manuscripts, and ancient versions render it differently (Septuagint has multiple variants), reflecting textual uncertainty. The name's etymology is unclear, possibly related to roots involving 'hire' or branches. Beyond this genealogical mention, nothing is known of this individual. The Benjaminite context places him within Saul's tribal lineage.

senses.1: 1 Chronicles 8:10 lists Sakhyah among Shaharaim's sons in the complex Benjaminite genealogy. The multilingual glosses show variation: Spanish 'Soquias,' reflecting different vocalization traditions. Ancient versions struggled with this name, producing multiple transliterations. The Chronicles genealogist includes such names to establish Benjaminite lineage comprehensively, even when individuals have no additional narrative role. These names preserve family memory and tribal identity, especially important for Benjamin after exile given the tribe's association with Saul and Jerusalem.

gloss_readable: This noun denotes rottenness or decay, appearing in Job 41:27 (English 41:19) where Leviathan regards iron as 'rotten wood'—utterly contemptible and ineffective. The term emphasizes advanced decomposition, wood so decayed it has lost all structural integrity. In this context, rottenness becomes a metaphor for worthlessness: even strong iron is, to Leviathan, as useless as punk wood. The multilingual evidence (Spanish 'podrida') consistently captures the decay aspect.

senses.1: Job 41:27 uses this vivid image in God's speech about Leviathan's invulnerability: to this creature, iron weapons are no more threatening than 'wood of rottenness.' The phrase evokes completely degraded timber—spongy, crumbling, powerless. Spanish 'podrida' (rotten) precisely captures the state. The rhetorical force lies in the reversal: iron, symbol of strength, is dismissed as thoroughly as decomposed wood. Leviathan's superiority makes the strong seem pathetically weak.

gloss_terse: Rakkon (place name: town in Dan's territory)
gloss_readable: This is a place name appearing in Joshua's boundary descriptions for the tribe of Dan (19:46). The site is likely identical with the nearby Yarkon, as suggested by the similar consonants and the fact that the Septuagint omits it (possibly viewing it as a textual variant). The exact location remains uncertain, though Jewish tradition later connected it with the region near Tiberias. The conjunction 'and' before the name integrates it into the boundary list.

senses.1: In Joshua 19:46, 'ha-Rakkon' appears in the territorial allotment for Dan, listed among cities and geographical features. Modern scholars see this as probably a doublet of 'the Yarkon' (the river that flows through modern Tel Aviv). The multilingual glosses preserve the Hebrew article 'ha-' and the name 'Rakkon,' treating it as a geographical designation rather than translating it. The uncertainty in ancient versions reflects early scribal puzzlement over this reference.

gloss_readable: This term refers to spiced or aromatic wine, appearing in Song of Songs 8:2 where the beloved speaks of giving her lover 'wine of spice'—wine infused with aromatic ingredients. Ancient spiced wines were prestigious luxury items, enhanced with various aromatics for flavor and fragrance. The definite article suggests a specific type: 'the spiced (wine).' This detail enriches the love poetry with sensory abundance: not plain wine but perfumed, carefully prepared wine, expressing lavish affection.

senses.1: In Song 8:2, 'the spiced' (with 'wine' implied or explicit) describes aromatic wine the bride would give her beloved. Spanish 'especiado' (spiced), French 'aromatisé' (aromatized), all capture the enhancement through aromatic additives. This was ancient viticulture's luxury product—wine improved with spices, creating complex flavors and fragrances. The context of extravagant love-language makes this detail fitting: the best, most carefully crafted refreshment for the beloved.

gloss_terse: perfumers, makers of ointments and fragrances (professional guild)
gloss_readable: This plural noun designates professional perfumers or ointment-makers, appearing in Nehemiah 3:8 where Hananiah 'son of the perfumers' (i.e., member of the perfumers' guild) helps rebuild Jerusalem's wall. The phrase 'son of the perfumers' indicates guild membership, a common way to denote professional association in ancient contexts. These artisans specialized in creating the precious oils, incenses, and perfumes essential for temple worship, royal courts, and daily life in the ancient Near East.

senses.1: Nehemiah 3:8 mentions 'one of the perfumers' (literally 'son of the perfumers'), identifying Hananiah by his professional guild. The multilingual glosses uniformly preserve the occupational designation: Spanish 'perfumeros,' English 'perfumers.' These specialists compounded the complex recipes for sacred anointing oil, incense, and cosmetic preparations. The detail that even perfumers joined the wall-building effort shows the comprehensive mobilization of Jerusalem's population for Nehemiah's restoration project.

gloss_readable: This plural noun refers to perfumes or fragrant ointments, appearing only in Isaiah 57:9 in a scathing denunciation of idolatry. The passage describes bringing perfumes (along with oil) to a pagan deity. The use of precious cosmetics in illicit worship heightens the prophetic critique—Israel lavishes on false gods the fragrances that should honor Yahweh alone. The second-person suffix ('your perfumes') personalizes the indictment, making the idolatry intimate and deliberate.

senses.1: Isaiah 57:9 condemns those who bring 'your perfumes' to idols, wasting precious aromatic preparations on false worship. Spanish 'tus perfumes' (your perfumes) preserves both the possessive and the plural. These would be expensive fragrant oils or ointments, valuable trade goods. The prophet's point cuts deep: Israel takes what should express devotion to God and instead offers it to worthless idols. The costly perfumes underscore the tragic misdirection of worship.

gloss_terse: perfumers (female), women who make fragrances and ointments
gloss_readable: This feminine plural noun designates female perfumers or ointment-makers, appearing in 1 Samuel 8:13 where Samuel warns that a future king will conscript Israelite daughters as perfumers, cooks, and bakers for the royal court. The grouping with other culinary and aromatic specialists suggests these women would produce the luxury goods required by monarchy—fragrant oils, cosmetics, and incense. The warning presents royal service as burdensome appropriation of family members.

senses.1: In 1 Samuel 8:13, Samuel's dire preview of kingship includes the seizure of daughters 'for perfumers, for cooks, and for bakers.' The Spanish 'para perfumeras' (for perfumers-feminine) preserves the gender specificity. These women would staff the royal production of fragrances and ointments, work that in household contexts women often managed. The threefold list (perfumers, cooks, bakers) evokes the extensive domestic infrastructure monarchy would require, transforming free daughters into royal servants.

gloss_readable: This plural construct noun refers to hammered or beaten-out metal plates, appearing in Numbers 16:38 (English 17:3) where the censers of Korah's rebels are to be hammered into sheets for plating the altar. The term emphasizes the process: metal beaten thin and wide, transformed from vessels into covering plates. This becomes a perpetual memorial—rebellion's instruments converted into sanctuary furnishings, warning against future presumption. The hammering itself is sacramental: judgment transformed into instruction.

senses.1: Numbers 16:38 commands that the bronze censers be made into 'hammered plates' (literally 'expansions of plates') to overlay the altar. The glosses emphasize the hammering process: Spanish 'láminas' (sheets/plates), English 'hammered.' The rebels' censers, used in unauthorized worship that brought death, become permanent altar covering—visible reminder that holiness cannot be presumed upon. The metal's transformation from censers to plates mirrors the narrative's transformation from rebellion to warning.

gloss_readable: This verb means to spit, appearing in Leviticus 15:8 in purity regulations: if a man with a discharge spits on someone clean, that person becomes unclean. Spitting here is not hostile but physiological—yet it transmits impurity. The law's precision about even saliva shows how comprehensively discharge-related uncleanness could spread. The regulation protects community health while maintaining ritual boundaries, treating spittle as a vector for contagion.

senses.1: Leviticus 15:8 addresses the scenario where 'the one with the discharge spits on the clean person'—direct transmission of impurity through saliva. The verb appears with the preposition 'upon,' indicating the target. Spanish 'escupiere' (should spit), English 'spits' capture the physiological act. This isn't contemptuous spitting (as in some other biblical contexts) but the ordinary expectoration that becomes significant because it carries ritual impurity from the diseased person to the clean.

gloss_terse: Rakkath (place name: fortified city in Naphtali's territory)
gloss_readable: This is a place name, one of the fortified cities in Naphtali's allotment (Joshua 19:35). Jewish tradition later identified it with Tiberias on the Sea of Galilee's western shore, though this identification remains uncertain. The Septuagint's variant spellings reflect ancient uncertainty about the exact location. As a fortified city, Rakkath would have been strategically important in Naphtali's northern territory, helping secure the tribe's holdings.

senses.1: Joshua 19:35 lists Rakkath among Naphtali's fortified cities, situated in the northern tribal territory. The multilingual glosses simply transliterate: Spanish 'Racat,' English 'Rakkath.' Later Jewish tradition connected this site with Tiberias, the important Galilean city that became a center of rabbinic learning. The Septuagint's various renderings suggest the translators struggled with this proper name. The designation 'fortified city' indicates Rakkath's strategic and defensive significance in Naphtali's territorial network.

gloss_readable: This noun means permission or authorization, appearing only in Ezra 3:7 where the returned exiles give money and provisions to workers 'according to the permission of Cyrus.' The term denotes official royal authorization—not mere tolerance but explicit grant. This legal precision matters in Ezra's narrative: the restoration happens not as rebellion but as imperially sanctioned project. The Persian king's written permission validates the temple rebuilding, protecting it from local opposition.

senses.1: Ezra 3:7 describes provision of supplies 'according to the grant of Cyrus king of Persia'—the royal authorization that legitimizes the entire restoration enterprise. Spanish 'según autorización' (according to authorization) captures the formal, legal character. This isn't informal approval but documented permission, likely referring to Cyrus's famous decree allowing the Jews to return and rebuild. The phrase grounds the restoration in official sanction, making opposition to it resistance to imperial policy.

gloss_readable: This passive participle means 'inscribed' or 'written down,' appearing in Daniel 10:21 where the angelic messenger tells Daniel he will declare 'what is inscribed in the writing of truth.' The term emphasizes permanent recording—not oral tradition but fixed text. The 'writing of truth' suggests an authoritative divine document, a heavenly archive where future events are already recorded. This apocalyptic image presents history as foreordained and documented, revelation as disclosure of what's already written.

senses.1: Daniel 10:21 speaks of 'that which is inscribed in the writing of truth'—the definite article marking this as a specific, authoritative text. Spanish 'lo escrito' (that which is written), French 'écrire' (to write), all emphasize the written, recorded nature. The passive participle suggests something already permanently documented. In apocalyptic literature, this imagery of heavenly books recording future events portrays divine sovereignty: history unfolds according to what's already inscribed in God's archive.

gloss_readable: This is a personal name appearing in 1 Chronicles 7:25, part of the genealogy of Ephraim. The name Resheph is identical to a common noun meaning 'flame' or 'burning,' and also to a West Semitic deity associated with plague and the underworld. Whether the personal name carries these associations or is simply a theophoric element is uncertain. The genealogical context situates this Resheph within Ephraim's lineage without additional biographical detail.

senses.1: In 1 Chronicles 7:25, Resheph appears as a descendant in Ephraim's genealogy, listed simply by name without further information. The Septuagint transliterates variously, reflecting the challenge of rendering Hebrew names into Greek. The name itself means 'flame' and was also a deity name in Canaanite religion, though in personal names such meanings often become merely conventional. The Chronicles genealogist includes Resheph to establish Ephraimite lineage, particularly leading toward Joshua (the chapter's climactic figure).

gloss_readable: This plural noun with suffix means 'its boilings,' appearing in Ezekiel 24:5 in a prophetic allegory where Jerusalem is depicted as a cooking pot. The command is to 'boil its boilings'—make it boil vigorously. However, BDB notes this is likely a textual corruption for 'its pieces' (the meat inside), which fits better with the cooking metaphor elsewhere in the chapter. The image of intense boiling suits the context of judgment: Jerusalem under siege is like a pot brought to furious, destructive boil.

senses.1: Ezekiel 24:5 uses this phrase in the extended metaphor of Jerusalem as a corroded pot on the fire: 'boil its boilings' or 'make it seethe vigorously.' Spanish 'hervores de ella' (its boilings) preserves the intensified action. Most scholars suspect textual corruption here (reading 'its pieces' instead), but the received text creates vivid image: repeated boiling, fierce heat, destructive intensity—all figuring the siege's relentless pressure. The cooking imagery throughout Ezekiel 24 turns domestic activity into vehicle for judgment oracle.

gloss_terse: harness, bind, attach (animals to a chariot)
gloss_readable: This verb means to harness or attach draft animals to a vehicle, appearing only in Micah 1:13: 'Harness the chariot to the horse.' The command is directed to Lachish in a context of judgment, possibly ironic—prepare to flee, or perhaps prepare for futile military response. The Arabic cognate suggests binding or tying as a reminder, and here the binding is the practical attachment of horse to chariot. The imperative creates urgency: action required in crisis.

senses.1: Micah 1:13 commands the inhabitants of Lachish: 'Harness the chariot to the swift steed.' Spanish 'Unce' (harness/yoke), English 'harness' capture the action of binding animal to vehicle. This could be preparation for flight or battle, though in context it appears futile—Lachish will fall despite chariots. The singular imperative personalizes the address, as if speaking to the city itself. The chariot imagery is bitterly appropriate: Lachish's military strength will not save it from the coming judgment.

gloss_readable: This plural construct noun refers to chains, appearing in Isaiah 40:19 in a description of idol-making: the craftsman overlays the idol with gold 'and chains of silver' (or possibly 'casts silver chains for it'). The context is satirical—the prophet mocks the elaborate process of manufacturing gods. Whether these chains are ornamental decoration or structural fasteners is unclear, but they represent additional costly materials lavished on worthless idols. The silver chains ironically bind not the idol but its deluded worshipers.

senses.1: Isaiah 40:19 describes idol manufacture, mentioning 'chains of silver' as part of the elaborate decoration. Spanish 'y cadenas' (and chains) preserves the connective and plural. The chains likely ornament the idol, adding silver to the gold overlay—expensive materials wasted on handmade deities. The prophet's rhetoric is devastating: such elaborate effort to create a god who can't speak, move, or save. The chains, meant to beautify, become symbols of the craftsmen's bondage to their own handiwork.

gloss_readable: This noun denotes trembling or terror, appearing in Hosea 13:1 in a difficult text: 'When Ephraim spoke, trembling' (or possibly 'spoke with trembling,' or 'spoke, there was trembling'). The verse contrasts Ephraim's former exalted status (when his words commanded fear/respect) with his subsequent guilt through Baal worship. Whether the trembling is Ephraim's own reverent fear or others' fearful response to his authority remains textually ambiguous, but the image evokes a time when Ephraim's leadership carried weight.

senses.1: Hosea 13:1 presents interpretive challenges, but describes a time 'when Ephraim spoke, trembling'—either Ephraim spoke with humble fear, or his speech inspired trembling in others. Spanish 'temblor,' French 'crainte' (fear) both capture the fearful aspect. The verse mourns Ephraim's fall from a state where speaking carried authority/reverence to one of death through idolatry. The trembling represents either proper fear before God (now abandoned) or commanding respect (now lost). Either way, it marks a vanished condition.

gloss_readable: This Hithpael participle means gazing or staring intently, appearing in Genesis 24:21 where Abraham's servant watches Rebekah closely at the well, silently assessing whether the Lord has made his journey successful. The intensive stem suggests sustained, focused attention—not a glance but a gaze. The servant's silence and steady watching create narrative tension: will this be the woman? The multilingual evidence consistently emphasizes the visual focus, the concentrated observation.

senses.1: Genesis 24:21 describes Abraham's servant 'gazing at her' (at Rebekah) after she has offered water to him and his camels—precisely the sign he requested. The Hithpael form intensifies the action: he's staring, watching intently, 'keeping silence to know whether the Lord had made his journey successful.' Spanish 'asombrado' (amazed) adds emotional dimension, though the verb primarily means to gaze steadily. This is the silent, hopeful scrutiny of someone watching for divine confirmation in human actions.

gloss_readable: This noun (Ketiv reading) refers to a devastating storm or ruin, appearing in Proverbs 1:27 where Wisdom warns that calamity will come 'like a storm.' The Qere reading prefers a different vocalization (שׁוֹאָה), but both point to destructive tempest. The image parallels 'whirlwind,' creating vivid picture of sudden, overwhelming disaster. Wisdom's discourse uses storm-language to warn the simple: reject instruction and calamity will strike with meteorological violence and inevitability.

senses.1: Proverbs 1:27 (Ketiv reading) warns that disaster will come upon the foolish 'like a devastating storm,' parallel with 'like a whirlwind.' The multilingual glosses mark this as a textual variant. The imagery is of sudden, irresistible destruction—storm as metaphor for calamity that sweeps away those who ignored Wisdom's call. Whether read as שַׁאֲוָה or שׁוֹאָה (Qere), the term evokes violent weather that obliterates everything in its path, suiting Wisdom's rhetoric of inevitable consequences.

gloss_terse: Shaulite (gentilic: descendants of Shaul, clan in Simeon)
gloss_readable: This is a gentilic adjective (with the definite article) functioning as a collective noun, referring to the Shaulite clan descended from Shaul within the tribe of Simeon. It appears in Numbers 26:13 in the wilderness census, where Israelite families are enumerated. The form follows standard patterns for clan designation, deriving from the ancestor's name with the -ite ending. The article makes it collective: 'the Shaulites' as a group.

senses.1: Numbers 26:13 lists 'the Shaulites' among Simeonite clans in the census. The multilingual glosses transliterate with the appropriate article: Spanish 'los saulitas' (the Shaulites), English 'the Shaulite.' This collective designation identifies all descendants of Shaul son of Simeon as a single clan unit for census and inheritance purposes. The census context makes clan membership crucial—these genealogical distinctions determined land allotment, military organization, and social identity in Israel.

gloss_readable: This noun means ruin or desolation, appearing in Isaiah 24:12, a late oracle depicting universal devastation: 'In the city is left desolation, and the gate is battered into ruin.' The term emphasizes the aftermath—not the destroying but the state of being destroyed. Isaiah 24's apocalyptic vision presents comprehensive collapse, and this word captures the endpoint: emptiness, wreckage, the stillness after catastrophe. The conjunction links this ruin to the broader scene of destruction.

senses.1: Isaiah 24:12 describes the ruined city's condition: 'In the city is left desolation, and the gate is battered into ruin.' Spanish 'y ruina' (and ruin) preserves the conjunction connecting this to the previous devastation. The term denotes the post-destruction state—the silence and emptiness after calamity. In Isaiah 24's cosmic judgment scene, this ruin is not one city's fate but representative of universal collapse. The battered gate particularly symbolizes failed defense, the city's protective boundary now rubble.

gloss_terse: Sheal (personal name: man who married foreign wife)
gloss_readable: This is a personal name appearing in Ezra 10:29, identifying one of the Israelites who had married foreign women during the exile and were required to divorce them in Ezra's reforms. The name itself means 'asking' or 'request.' Beyond this single mention in the list of those with foreign wives, nothing else is known about this individual. The Septuagint renders it variously, reflecting the challenges of transliterating Hebrew names.

senses.1: Ezra 10:29 lists Sheal among those who 'had taken foreign wives'—the controversial marriages Ezra demanded be dissolved to maintain covenant purity. The name appears with the conjunction 'and,' integrating it into the catalog of offenders. German 'und fragte' (and asked) attempts to translate the name's meaning rather than transliterate, showing the semantic root. The list itself is painful: names without stories, men whose personal lives became battleground in the community's struggle to maintain distinct identity after exile.

gloss_readable: This Aramaic noun means request, petition, or affair, appearing in Daniel 4:17 (Aramaic 4:14) in Nebuchadnezzar's dream decree: 'This sentence is by the decree of the watchers, the decision by the word of the holy ones, to the intent that the living may know...' The emphatic form (with Aramaic definite article) marks this as 'the request/matter at hand.' The term has shifted from 'question' to 'affair' or 'matter'—the issue being decided, the case under consideration.

senses.1: Daniel 4:17 (Aramaic section) uses this term for 'the request' or 'the matter' decreed by the heavenly watchers—the sentence upon Nebuchadnezzar. Spanish 'la demanda' (the petition/request), English 'the request' both preserve the definite article. Though the root means 'ask' or 'inquire,' here it's weakened to mean 'affair' or 'matter'—the business at hand. The heavenly council's decree becomes a legal petition presented to the living: this judgment demonstrates that the Most High rules over human kingdoms.

gloss_readable: This personal name means 'I have asked God' or 'God's request,' appearing frequently in post-exilic texts as the father of Zerubbabel, the governor who led the return from Babylon. Ezra 5:2 specifically mentions Shealtiel in connection with the temple rebuilding. The name's theophoric element (containing 'El' = God) reflects piety and dependence. Shealtiel's prominence derives from his son Zerubbabel, the Davidic heir who became focal point for messianic hopes during the restoration.

senses.1: Ezra 5:2 identifies Zerubbabel as 'son of Shealtiel,' the genealogical connection establishing Davidic lineage and legitimacy for leadership. The multilingual glosses transliterate the name: Spanish 'Salatiel,' English 'Shealtiel,' German 'Schealtiel.' Shealtiel appears in both Ezra-Nehemiah and Haggai-Zechariah as Zerubbabel's father, anchoring the governor's authority in Davidic descent. The name itself ('I have asked God') may reflect circumstances of his birth or his parents' piety, a permanent testimony to dependence on divine providence.

gloss_readable: This Qal participle with second feminine suffix means 'those plundering you,' appearing in Jeremiah 30:16 in an oracle of reversal: 'All who devour you shall be devoured, and all your foes shall go into captivity; those who plunder you shall become plunder.' The verb denotes violent seizure and despoiling. The poetic justice is perfect: the plunderers will be plundered. This Ketiv form is marked as Aramaic spelling, showing linguistic influence during the exilic period.

senses.1: Jeremiah 30:16 promises reversal of Israel's suffering: 'those plundering you shall become plunder.' The participle with suffix personalizes the promise—'YOUR plunderers' will face their own despoiling. This is the lex talionis applied to nations: the violence done to Israel will return upon the perpetrators. The Aramaic spelling (Ketiv, versus Hebrew Qere) reflects the linguistic environment of the exile, when Aramaic increasingly influenced Hebrew. The promise offers hope: current plundering is not final; the plunderers face divine judgment.

gloss_terse: flesh, meat; near kin, blood relative
gloss_readable: This noun means flesh, used both literally (as meat or bodily flesh) and figuratively (as blood relation). In Leviticus 18:17 it appears in the prohibition against marrying both a woman and her daughter: 'they are her near relatives'—literally 'her flesh.' The term emphasizes the physical, biological connection—shared blood and kinship. The marriage prohibitions in Leviticus 18 repeatedly invoke this language of 'flesh,' treating sexual relations with close kin as violations of fundamental boundaries.

senses.1: Leviticus 18:17 forbids marrying a woman and her daughter because 'they are her near relatives'—literally 'they are her flesh.' The phrase establishes blood connection as the reason for prohibition: these relationships are too close, the shared kinship creating incestuous overlap. Spanish 'su carne' (her flesh) preserves the literal Hebrew. This usage extends 'flesh' from physical substance to kinship category, treating biological connection as defining relational boundaries. The flesh-language makes abstract kinship viscerally concrete.

gloss_terse: Sheerah (personal name: daughter of Ephraim or his descendant)
gloss_readable: This is a feminine personal name appearing in 1 Chronicles 7:24, identifying a daughter (or female descendant) of Ephraim who built three towns: Lower and Upper Beth-horon and Uzzen-sheerah. She is the only woman in biblical genealogies credited with founding cities, making her remarkable. The name may be related to the word for 'flesh' or 'kinship,' though its precise etymology is uncertain. The Septuagint struggled with this name, rendering it variously.

senses.1: 1 Chronicles 7:24 identifies Sheerah as Ephraim's daughter who 'built Lower and Upper Beth-horon, and Uzzen-sheerah.' The multilingual glosses transliterate: Spanish 'Seera,' English 'Sheerah.' This unique notice makes Sheerah extraordinary in biblical record—a woman credited with founding multiple settlements. Whether biological daughter or more distant descendant is debated, but the text honors her as builder and founder. Uzzen-sheerah ('ear/corner of Sheerah') perpetuates her name geographically, rare recognition for a woman's accomplishment.

gloss_readable: This is the symbolic name of Isaiah's son, appearing in Isaiah 7:3 where God commands the prophet to take this son when confronting King Ahaz. The name means 'a remnant shall return,' embodying Isaiah's theology of judgment and hope—though most will be destroyed, a faithful remnant will survive and return. The child becomes a walking prophecy, his very name proclaiming both threat and promise every time it's spoken. Such naming makes theology incarnate.

senses.1: Isaiah 7:3 introduces 'Shear-jashub your son' whom Isaiah must bring to meet Ahaz during the Syro-Ephraimite crisis. The name means 'a remnant shall return,' a compressed theology: judgment will come but not total annihilation; a purified remnant will survive. The multilingual glosses preserve the Hebrew name untranslated (Spanish 'Shear-Yashub'), recognizing it as proper name with embedded meaning. The son's presence physically embodies the prophetic message: faith or fear? The name confronts Ahaz with both warning and hope.

gloss_readable: This noun's meaning is disputed—possibly devastation or the din/tumult of battle. It appears in Lamentations 3:47, paired with 'ruin' in the poet's lament: 'Terror and the pit have come upon us, devastation and destruction.' The parallelism with 'ruin' suggests catastrophic disaster. Some derive it from roots meaning 'battle-din' or 'uproar,' others from roots meaning 'desolation.' Either sense fits Lamentations' context of Jerusalem's fall. The uncertainty reflects textual difficulty and the word's rarity.

senses.1: Lamentations 3:47 pairs this term with 'ruin' in catalog of disasters: 'fear and the pit, devastation and destruction' (or possibly 'tumult and ruin'). The definite article marks it as specific catastrophe—THE devastation. Whether understanding it as 'battle-din' (the terrible noise of conquest) or 'devastation' (the resulting desolation), the context is Jerusalem's destruction. The poet piles up disaster-terms, and this word—whatever its precise nuance—adds to the overwhelming sense of comprehensive calamity.

gloss_terse: Sabeans (gentilic: people from Sheba, in Arabia)
gloss_readable: This gentilic plural refers to the Sabeans, people from Sheba in southwestern Arabia (modern Yemen), appearing in Joel 3:8 in an oracle of judgment: Israel's oppressors will be sold 'to the Sabeans, to a nation far away.' The Sabeans were known for trade, especially in spices and precious goods. The irony: those who enslaved Israel will themselves be sold to distant traders. The phrase 'far away' emphasizes exile and distance—the oppressors will experience the displacement they inflicted.

senses.1: Joel 3:8 (English 4:8) declares that Judah and Jerusalem will sell their enemies 'to the Sabeans, to a nation far away'—the slave trade reversed. Spanish 'a sabeos' (to Sabeans), French 'Sabéen' preserve the gentilic designation. The Sabeans, from southwestern Arabia, were merchants and traders; being sold to them means entering the international slave trade, experiencing the commodity status Israel suffered. The geographic distance ('far away') compounds the judgment: total removal from homeland, ironic reversal of the scattering inflicted on God's people.

gloss_readable: This plural noun probably means splinters or fragments, appearing in Hosea 8:6 in judgment against the golden calf of Samaria: 'it shall be broken in pieces' (literally 'it shall become splinters'). The image is of complete fragmentation—the idol reduced to shards and fragments, utterly destroyed. The term evokes not just breaking but disintegration into many small pieces. The golden calf, crafted by human hands, will be smashed into splinters, demonstrating its utter powerlessness.

senses.1: Hosea 8:6 pronounces doom on Samaria's calf-idol: 'it shall become splinters'—complete fragmentation. Spanish 'pedazos' (pieces/fragments) captures the multiplication of broken parts. The image reverses creation: what craftsmen assembled will be shattered into countless fragments. The splinters represent both physical destruction and theological point—this 'god' crafted from precious metal has no divine substance, just material that breaks. The calf's fate as splinters mocks the worship that treated metal as deity.

gloss_readable: This is the Aramaic plural construct for 'tribes,' appearing in Ezra 6:17 in the account of the second temple's dedication, where sacrifices are offered 'for all Israel, twelve he-goats, according to the number of the tribes of Israel.' The Aramaic form appears in the Aramaic section of Ezra, though the concept mirrors Hebrew usage. The twelve-tribe structure remains fundamental even after exile, the ritual acknowledging all Israel despite the physical return of only some tribes.

senses.1: Ezra 6:17 describes dedication sacrifices 'according to the number of the tribes of Israel'—twelve he-goats for twelve tribes. The multilingual glosses preserve the construct form: Spanish 'las tribus de' (the tribes of). This is Aramaic equivalent of Hebrew 'tribes,' appearing in Ezra's Aramaic section. The twelve-fold sacrifice honors the ideal of all Israel, even though only Judah, Benjamin, and some Levites returned. The ritual asserts continuity: despite exile and decimation, Israel remains the twelve-tribe people of covenant.

gloss_readable: This is the name of the eleventh month in the post-exilic calendar, corresponding roughly to February-March. It appears in Zechariah 1:7, dating a vision 'on the twenty-fourth day of the eleventh month, which is the month Shebat.' This is a Babylonian loan-word, adopted during the exile to replace earlier Hebrew month names. The etymology possibly relates to Akkadian words for striking or destroying (referring to destructive winter rains), though this remains uncertain.

senses.1: Zechariah 1:7 dates a prophetic vision 'in the month Shebat, which is the eleventh month'—mid-winter in the second year of Darius. The multilingual glosses transliterate: Spanish 'Sebat,' French 'Schebat.' This Babylonian month name replaced earlier Hebrew designations, linguistic evidence of exile's cultural impact. The month falls in winter's heart, when destructive rains dominate Palestine. Zechariah's visions come during this dark, wet season, the timing perhaps reflecting Israel's own dark season of subjugation and partial restoration.

gloss_terse: captive (feminine adjective, describing one in captivity)
gloss_readable: This feminine adjective means 'captive,' appearing in Isaiah 52:2 in an imperative to personified Jerusalem: 'Shake yourself from the dust, arise, O captive Jerusalem!' The feminine form matches 'daughter of Zion,' treating the city as a woman in bondage who must now assert her freedom. The term emphasizes state not just event—not the act of capturing but the condition of being captive. The command to 'arise' and shake off dust calls the captive to agency and restoration.

senses.1: Isaiah 52:2 (based on textual emendation) addresses Jerusalem as 'captive daughter of Zion,' calling her to rise from the dust. The feminine adjective 'captive' matches the feminine personification of the city. Spanish 'cautiva' preserves the gender. The passage demands action from the captive: though enslaved, Jerusalem must now shake off the bonds and dust, asserting freedom in response to God's deliverance. The captive state is real but not final—the call to 'arise' transforms passive victim into active participant in liberation.

gloss_terse: Shobi (personal name: Ammonite who aided David)
gloss_readable: This personal name identifies an Ammonite who brought supplies to David when he fled from Absalom, appearing in 2 Samuel 17:27. Shobi son of Nahash from Rabbah of the Ammonites joined Barzillai and Machir in provisioning David's company during the rebellion. His Ammonite identity is striking—a foreigner showing loyalty when David's own son rebelled. The name may relate to 'captive' or 'captivity,' though its precise meaning is uncertain.

senses.1: 2 Samuel 17:27 lists Shobi among three men who brought essential supplies to David at Mahanaim during Absalom's revolt. The Septuagint renders the name variously, struggling with the Hebrew. What's remarkable is Shobi's Ammonite identity—traditional enemy showing compassion to David in crisis. This foreigner's loyalty contrasts sharply with Israelite Absalom's rebellion. The conjunction 'and Shobi' integrates him into the list of benefactors, honored in Scripture for kindness when David most needed it.

gloss_readable: This noun means flame or blaze, appearing in Job 18:5 in Bildad's description of the wicked person's fate: 'the light of the wicked is put out, and the flame of his fire does not shine.' The parallel structure equates 'light' with 'flame,' both representing the wicked person's life or prosperity. The construct form 'flame of his fire' emphasizes the burning aspect—not just fire but its bright, active flame. The extinction of this flame pictures complete cessation of the wicked person's vitality.

senses.1: Job 18:5 declares that 'the flame of his fire shall not shine,' parallel with 'the light of the wicked goes out.' Spanish 'chispa de' (spark of) varies slightly, but the image is of flame extinguished—the bright, dancing fire reduced to nothing. The construct 'flame of his fire' intensifies the loss: not just fire dimming but its very flame—the most visible, energetic part—disappearing. In wisdom literature, such extinction metaphorically represents death or divine judgment cutting off the wicked person's life and legacy.

gloss_readable: This personal name appears in 1 Chronicles 8:10 in the genealogy of Benjamin, listed among the sons of Shaharaim. The name's spelling varies in manuscripts, and ancient versions render it differently (Septuagint has multiple variants), reflecting textual uncertainty. The name's etymology is unclear, possibly related to roots involving 'hire' or branches. Beyond this genealogical mention, nothing is known of this individual. The Benjaminite context places him within Saul's tribal lineage.

senses.1: 1 Chronicles 8:10 lists Sakhyah among Shaharaim's sons in the complex Benjaminite genealogy. The multilingual glosses show variation: Spanish 'Soquias,' reflecting different vocalization traditions. Ancient versions struggled with this name, producing multiple transliterations. The Chronicles genealogist includes such names to establish Benjaminite lineage comprehensively, even when individuals have no additional narrative role. These names preserve family memory and tribal identity, especially important for Benjamin after exile given the tribe's association with Saul and Jerusalem.
